analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover mental health care on the same terms as physical health care.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the Mental Health Parity Act of 2007 unanimously with 58 senators signed on, but it died in two House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employer health plans that cover mental health and substance use treatment to apply the same deductibles, copayments, and visit limits to those benefits as to medical and surgical care — including out-of-network care. It exempted employers with 50 or fewer workers, let plans off the hook for a year if costs rose more than a set threshold, and created ombudsmen and random audits to enforce compliance. It passed the Senate unanimously but never received a vote in the House, sitting in committee until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families with employer health plans at companies with more than 50 employees, especially people who use mental health or substance use treatment. They would no longer face higher copays, separate deductibles, or strict caps on therapy visits and inpatient days that do not apply to physical health care. Mental health and addiction treatment providers would also gain, since more patients could afford and continue care.

how_it_helps.text: Outlaws higher deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, out-of-pocket costs, and annual or lifetime limits for mental health benefits than what medical and surgical benefits carry — and bans separate cost-sharing rules that apply only to mental health.
Extends the parity guarantee to out-of-network mental health care, not just in-network care, if the plan offers both.
Ends tight caps on the number of therapy visits or days of inpatient treatment that are stricter than the limits applied to medical and surgical care.
Creates ombudsmen at the Labor and Health and Human Services Departments to help people with coverage questions, and requires random audits of group health plans to check compliance.
Requires a GAO study of the law's effect on insurance costs, access, and quality of care, and requires final regulations within one year of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and large employers, who would bear the cost of equalized mental health benefits and compliance with audits and reporting. The bill cushions them: small employers are exempt, and any plan whose total coverage costs rise more than 2 percent the first year or 1 percent after can skip the requirement for a year. Premiums for covered workers could rise somewhat if mental health use increases.

drawbacks.text: Plans may keep managing mental health care their own way — utilization review, prior authorization, narrower provider networks, and separate reimbursement rates — so parity in cost-sharing does not guarantee equal access to care in practice.

A plan can escape the requirement entirely for a year if a certified actuary finds that parity raises total coverage costs by more than 2 percent in the first year or 1 percent thereafter, and the underlying data is a narrow band of insurers, employers, and actuaries.

Employers with 50 or fewer employees are exempt, and the bill preempts state parity laws for large employers except in the individual and small-group markets, potentially wiping out stronger state protections.
The bill requires parity only if a plan already offers mental health benefits; it does not require any plan to cover mental health or substance use treatment at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were real and broad: tens of millions of workers in large group plans would have gained equal deductibles, copays, and visit limits for mental health and substance use care, backed by audits and an ombudsman. The costs were contained by design — the bill applied only to employers with more than 50 employees, did not require any plan to offer mental health benefits in the first place, and let plans escape for a year if a certified actuary showed cost increases above 1–2 percent. The serious weaknesses are that the cost escape hatch and the carve-out for managed care could blunt the guarantee in practice, and preemption could override stronger state parity mandates for large employers. On balance a modestly designed but genuinely helpful bill; the greater cost was that it never received a House vote at all.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously in September 2007, but the House referred it to two committees and their subcommittees, where it sat until Congress ended, so it never came up for a House vote.

narrative.text: The bill had 57 cosponsors — 38 Democrats, 18 Republicans, and 1 Independent — in addition to its Republican sponsor, giving it the backing of 58 of 100 senators.
The Senate HELP Committee reported the bill favorably on March 27, 2007, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
On September 18, 2007, the Senate took up the bill by unanimous consent and passed it with an amendment, with no recorded dissent.

The House referred the Senate bill to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor Committees on September 19, 2007, and then to subcommittees in September and October; no committee or floor action followed.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with the bill still pending in House subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For the remainder of the 110th Congress, health plans and large employers benefited from keeping the older, weaker parity rules that allowed stricter cost-sharing and visit limits on mental health care. A successor parity bill did become law later in 2008.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and large employers, for one more year

for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with an amendment in March 2007, filed the committee report, and brought it to the Senate floor, where it passed by unanimous consent.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the Senate-passed bill on September 19, 2007, referred it to the Subcommittee on Health, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the Senate-passed bill for portions under its jurisdiction, referred it to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions in October 2007, and never reported it or brought it to a vote.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule floor action on the Senate bill, advancing its own mental health parity bill instead; a successor parity law was enacted before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan: 38 Democrats, 18 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsored the bill alongside its Republican sponsor, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent.

industries.note: Insurers would lose the ability to charge higher cost-sharing and impose tighter visit and day limits on mental health benefits, and would face random compliance audits. The cost exemption gives them a yearly escape if costs rise more than 1–2 percent, and the bill is careful to preserve their managed-care and network practices.

Employers with more than 50 employees could see premiums rise if expanded mental health coverage increases claims, but the actuarial cost exemption lets them suspend parity for a year if costs exceed the threshold. They gain a healthier, more productive workforce in exchange.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance use treatment providers
industries.note: Therapists, psychiatrists, and addiction treatment programs would see demand rise as visit caps and higher copays fall away, making care easier for patients to afford and continue.
Every plan seeking the cost exemption must obtain a written certification from a qualified actuary, creating a new paid role for the profession.
